desc:
A sorted array of distinct integers was cut at some position into a front part and a back part, and the two parts were swapped. For instance [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] may become [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Cutting at the very end (or the very start) leaves the array unchanged.

Given such an array nums and an integer k, return the k-th smallest value, counting from 1. You may not sort the array: use O(log n) time. For nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] and k = 3 the answer is 2.
hints: Sorting works but costs O(n log n). The array is already almost sorted, so what information is missing?
If you knew the index where the sorted order starts (the index of the minimum), the k-th smallest would be exactly k - 1 places after it.
Find the index s of the minimum with a binary search, then answer nums[(s + k - 1) % n]; the modulo handles the wrap-around.
editorial: Reading the array circularly starting at the minimum gives the sorted order. So once the index s of the minimum is known, the k-th smallest is at (s + k - 1) mod n.

Find s with the usual binary search on a window [lo, hi]: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] the minimum lies right of mid (lo = mid + 1), otherwise at mid or left (hi = mid). This costs O(log n); the lookup afterwards is O(1). Space O(1).
